[130](https://docs.rs#130)    ($quote:item) => {
[131](https://docs.rs#131)        /// The whole point.
[132](https://docs.rs#132)        ///
[133](https://docs.rs#133)        /// Performs variable interpolation against the input and produces it as
[134](https://docs.rs#134)        /// [`proc_macro2::TokenStream`].
[135](https://docs.rs#135)        ///
[136](https://docs.rs#136)        /// Note: for returning tokens to the compiler in a procedural macro, use
[137](https://docs.rs#137)        /// `.into()` on the result to convert to [`proc_macro::TokenStream`].
[138](https://docs.rs#138)        ///
[139](https://docs.rs#139)        /// <br>
[140](https://docs.rs#140)        ///
[141](https://docs.rs#141)        /// # Interpolation
[142](https://docs.rs#142)        ///
[143](https://docs.rs#143)        /// Variable interpolation is done with `#var` (similar to `$var` in
[144](https://docs.rs#144)        /// `macro_rules!` macros). This grabs the `var` variable that is currently in
[145](https://docs.rs#145)        /// scope and inserts it in that location in the output tokens. Any type
[146](https://docs.rs#146)        /// implementing the [`ToTokens`] trait can be interpolated. This includes most
[147](https://docs.rs#147)        /// Rust primitive types as well as most of the syntax tree types from the [Syn]
[148](https://docs.rs#148)        /// crate.
[149](https://docs.rs#149)        ///
[150](https://docs.rs#150)        /// [Syn]: https://github.com/dtolnay/syn
[151](https://docs.rs#151)        ///
[152](https://docs.rs#152)        /// Repetition is done using `#(...)*` or `#(...),*` again similar to
[153](https://docs.rs#153)        /// `macro_rules!`. This iterates through the elements of any variable
[154](https://docs.rs#154)        /// interpolated within the repetition and inserts a copy of the repetition body
[155](https://docs.rs#155)        /// for each one. The variables in an interpolation may be a `Vec`, slice,
[156](https://docs.rs#156)        /// `BTreeSet`, or any `Iterator`.
[157](https://docs.rs#157)        ///
[158](https://docs.rs#158)        /// - `#(#var)*` — no separators
[159](https://docs.rs#159)        /// - `#(#var),*` — the character before the asterisk is used as a separator
[160](https://docs.rs#160)        /// - `#( struct #var; )*` — the repetition can contain other tokens
[161](https://docs.rs#161)        /// - `#( #k => println!("{}", #v), )*` — even multiple interpolations
[162](https://docs.rs#162)        ///
[163](https://docs.rs#163)        /// <br>
[164](https://docs.rs#164)        ///
[165](https://docs.rs#165)        /// # Hygiene
[166](https://docs.rs#166)        ///
[167](https://docs.rs#167)        /// Any interpolated tokens preserve the `Span` information provided by their
[168](https://docs.rs#168)        /// `ToTokens` implementation. Tokens that originate within the `quote!`
[169](https://docs.rs#169)        /// invocation are spanned with [`Span::call_site()`].
[170](https://docs.rs#170)        ///
[171](https://docs.rs#171)        /// [`Span::call_site()`]: proc_macro2::Span::call_site
[172](https://docs.rs#172)        ///
[173](https://docs.rs#173)        /// A different span can be provided through the [`quote_spanned!`] macro.
[174](https://docs.rs#174)        ///
[175](https://docs.rs#175)        /// <br>
[176](https://docs.rs#176)        ///
[177](https://docs.rs#177)        /// # Return type
[178](https://docs.rs#178)        ///
[179](https://docs.rs#179)        /// The macro evaluates to an expression of type `proc_macro2::TokenStream`.
[180](https://docs.rs#180)        /// Meanwhile Rust procedural macros are expected to return the type
[181](https://docs.rs#181)        /// `proc_macro::TokenStream`.
[182](https://docs.rs#182)        ///
[183](https://docs.rs#183)        /// The difference between the two types is that `proc_macro` types are entirely
[184](https://docs.rs#184)        /// specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a
[185](https://docs.rs#185)        /// procedural macro, while `proc_macro2` types may exist anywhere including
[186](https://docs.rs#186)        /// tests and non-macro code like main.rs and build.rs. This is why even the
[187](https://docs.rs#187)        /// procedural macro ecosystem is largely built around `proc_macro2`, because
[188](https://docs.rs#188)        /// that ensures the libraries are unit testable and accessible in non-macro
[189](https://docs.rs#189)        /// contexts.
[190](https://docs.rs#190)        ///
[191](https://docs.rs#191)        /// There is a [`From`]-conversion in both directions so returning the output of
[192](https://docs.rs#192)        /// `quote!` from a procedural macro usually looks like `tokens.into()` or
[193](https://docs.rs#193)        /// `proc_macro::TokenStream::from(tokens)`.
[194](https://docs.rs#194)        ///
[195](https://docs.rs#195)        /// <br>
[196](https://docs.rs#196)        ///
[197](https://docs.rs#197)        /// # Examples
[198](https://docs.rs#198)        ///
[199](https://docs.rs#199)        /// ### Procedural macro
[200](https://docs.rs#200)        ///
[201](https://docs.rs#201)        /// The structure of a basic procedural macro is as follows. Refer to the [Syn]
[202](https://docs.rs#202)        /// crate for further useful guidance on using `quote!` as part of a procedural
[203](https://docs.rs#203)        /// macro.
[204](https://docs.rs#204)        ///
[205](https://docs.rs#205)        /// [Syn]: https://github.com/dtolnay/syn
[206](https://docs.rs#206)        ///
[207](https://docs.rs#207)        /// ```
[208](https://docs.rs#208)        /// # #[cfg(any())]
[209](https://docs.rs#209)        /// extern crate proc_macro;
[210](https://docs.rs#210)        /// # extern crate proc_macro2;
[211](https://docs.rs#211)        ///
[212](https://docs.rs#212)        /// # #[cfg(any())]
[213](https://docs.rs#213)        /// use proc_macro::TokenStream;
[214](https://docs.rs#214)        /// # use proc_macro2::TokenStream;
[215](https://docs.rs#215)        /// use quote::quote;
[216](https://docs.rs#216)        ///
[217](https://docs.rs#217)        /// # const IGNORE_TOKENS: &'static str = stringify! {
[218](https://docs.rs#218)        /// #[proc_macro_derive(HeapSize)]
[219](https://docs.rs#219)        /// # };
[220](https://docs.rs#220)        /// pub fn derive_heap_size(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
[221](https://docs.rs#221)        ///     // Parse the input and figure out what implementation to generate...
[222](https://docs.rs#222)        ///     # const IGNORE_TOKENS: &'static str = stringify! {
[223](https://docs.rs#223)        ///     let name = /* ... */;
[224](https://docs.rs#224)        ///     let expr = /* ... */;
[225](https://docs.rs#225)        ///     # };
[226](https://docs.rs#226)        ///     #
[227](https://docs.rs#227)        ///     # let name = 0;
[228](https://docs.rs#228)        ///     # let expr = 0;
[229](https://docs.rs#229)        ///
[230](https://docs.rs#230)        ///     let expanded = quote! {
[231](https://docs.rs#231)        ///         // The generated impl.
[232](https://docs.rs#232)        ///         impl heapsize::HeapSize for #name {
[233](https://docs.rs#233)        ///             fn heap_size_of_children(&self) -> usize {
[234](https://docs.rs#234)        ///                 #expr
[235](https://docs.rs#235)        ///             }
[236](https://docs.rs#236)        ///         }
[237](https://docs.rs#237)        ///     };
[238](https://docs.rs#238)        ///
[239](https://docs.rs#239)        ///     // Hand the output tokens back to the compiler.
[240](https://docs.rs#240)        ///     TokenStream::from(expanded)
[241](https://docs.rs#241)        /// }
[242](https://docs.rs#242)        /// ```
[243](https://docs.rs#243)        ///
[244](https://docs.rs#244)        /// <p><br></p>
[245](https://docs.rs#245)        ///
[246](https://docs.rs#246)        /// ### Combining quoted fragments
[247](https://docs.rs#247)        ///
[248](https://docs.rs#248)        /// Usually you don't end up constructing an entire final `TokenStream` in one
[249](https://docs.rs#249)        /// piece. Different parts may come from different helper functions. The tokens
[250](https://docs.rs#250)        /// produced by `quote!` themselves implement `ToTokens` and so can be
[251](https://docs.rs#251)        /// interpolated into later `quote!` invocations to build up a final result.
[252](https://docs.rs#252)        ///
[253](https://docs.rs#253)        /// ```
[254](https://docs.rs#254)        /// # use quote::quote;
[255](https://docs.rs#255)        /// #
[256](https://docs.rs#256)        /// let type_definition = quote! {...};
[257](https://docs.rs#257)        /// let methods = quote! {...};
[258](https://docs.rs#258)        ///
[259](https://docs.rs#259)        /// let tokens = quote! {
[260](https://docs.rs#260)        ///     #type_definition
[261](https://docs.rs#261)        ///     #methods
[262](https://docs.rs#262)        /// };
[263](https://docs.rs#263)        /// ```
[264](https://docs.rs#264)        ///
[265](https://docs.rs#265)        /// <p><br></p>
[266](https://docs.rs#266)        ///
[267](https://docs.rs#267)        /// ### Constructing identifiers
[268](https://docs.rs#268)        ///
[269](https://docs.rs#269)        /// Suppose we have an identifier `ident` which came from somewhere in a macro
[270](https://docs.rs#270)        /// input and we need to modify it in some way for the macro output. Let's
[271](https://docs.rs#271)        /// consider prepending the identifier with an underscore.
[272](https://docs.rs#272)        ///
[273](https://docs.rs#273)        /// Simply interpolating the identifier next to an underscore will not have the
[274](https://docs.rs#274)        /// behavior of concatenating them. The underscore and the identifier will
[275](https://docs.rs#275)        /// continue to be two separate tokens as if you had written `_ x`.
[276](https://docs.rs#276)        ///
[277](https://docs.rs#277)        /// ```edition2018
[278](https://docs.rs#278)        /// # use proc_macro2::{self as syn, Span};
[279](https://docs.rs#279)        /// # use quote::quote;
[280](https://docs.rs#280)        /// #
[281](https://docs.rs#281)        /// # let ident = syn::Ident::new("i", Span::call_site());
[282](https://docs.rs#282)        /// #
[283](https://docs.rs#283)        /// // incorrect
[284](https://docs.rs#284)        /// quote! {
[285](https://docs.rs#285)        ///     let mut _#ident = 0;
[286](https://docs.rs#286)        /// }
[287](https://docs.rs#287)        /// # ;
[288](https://docs.rs#288)        /// ```
[289](https://docs.rs#289)        ///
[290](https://docs.rs#290)        /// The solution is to build a new identifier token with the correct value. As
[291](https://docs.rs#291)        /// this is such a common case, the [`format_ident!`] macro provides a
[292](https://docs.rs#292)        /// convenient utility for doing so correctly.
[293](https://docs.rs#293)        ///
[294](https://docs.rs#294)        /// ```
[295](https://docs.rs#295)        /// # use proc_macro2::{Ident, Span};
[296](https://docs.rs#296)        /// # use quote::{format_ident, quote};
[297](https://docs.rs#297)        /// #
[298](https://docs.rs#298)        /// # let ident = Ident::new("i", Span::call_site());
[299](https://docs.rs#299)        /// #
[300](https://docs.rs#300)        /// let varname = format_ident!("_{}", ident);
[301](https://docs.rs#301)        /// quote! {
[302](https://docs.rs#302)        ///     let mut #varname = 0;
[303](https://docs.rs#303)        /// }
[304](https://docs.rs#304)        /// # ;
[305](https://docs.rs#305)        /// ```
[306](https://docs.rs#306)        ///
[307](https://docs.rs#307)        /// Alternatively, the APIs provided by Syn and proc-macro2 can be used to
[308](https://docs.rs#308)        /// directly build the identifier. This is roughly equivalent to the above, but
[309](https://docs.rs#309)        /// will not handle `ident` being a raw identifier.
[310](https://docs.rs#310)        ///
[311](https://docs.rs#311)        /// ```
[312](https://docs.rs#312)        /// # use proc_macro2::{self as syn, Span};
[313](https://docs.rs#313)        /// # use quote::quote;
[314](https://docs.rs#314)        /// #
[315](https://docs.rs#315)        /// # let ident = syn::Ident::new("i", Span::call_site());
[316](https://docs.rs#316)        /// #
[317](https://docs.rs#317)        /// let concatenated = format!("_{}", ident);
[318](https://docs.rs#318)        /// let varname = syn::Ident::new(&concatenated, ident.span());
[319](https://docs.rs#319)        /// quote! {
[320](https://docs.rs#320)        ///     let mut #varname = 0;
[321](https://docs.rs#321)        /// }
[322](https://docs.rs#322)        /// # ;
[323](https://docs.rs#323)        /// ```
[324](https://docs.rs#324)        ///
[325](https://docs.rs#325)        /// <p><br></p>
[326](https://docs.rs#326)        ///
[327](https://docs.rs#327)        /// ### Making method calls
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        ///
[329](https://docs.rs#329)        /// Let's say our macro requires some type specified in the macro input to have
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        /// a constructor called `new`. We have the type in a variable called
[331](https://docs.rs#331)        /// `field_type` of type `syn::Type` and want to invoke the constructor.
[332](https://docs.rs#332)        ///
[333](https://docs.rs#333)        /// ```
[334](https://docs.rs#334)        /// # use quote::quote;
[335](https://docs.rs#335)        /// #
[336](https://docs.rs#336)        /// # let field_type = quote!(...);
[337](https://docs.rs#337)        /// #
[338](https://docs.rs#338)        /// // incorrect
[339](https://docs.rs#339)        /// quote! {
[340](https://docs.rs#340)        ///     let value = #field_type::new();
[341](https://docs.rs#341)        /// }
[342](https://docs.rs#342)        /// # ;
[343](https://docs.rs#343)        /// ```
[344](https://docs.rs#344)        ///
[345](https://docs.rs#345)        /// This works only sometimes. If `field_type` is `String`, the expanded code
[346](https://docs.rs#346)        /// contains `String::new()` which is fine. But if `field_type` is something
[347](https://docs.rs#347)        /// like `Vec<i32>` then the expanded code is `Vec<i32>::new()` which is invalid
[348](https://docs.rs#348)        /// syntax. Ordinarily in handwritten Rust we would write `Vec::<i32>::new()`
[349](https://docs.rs#349)        /// but for macros often the following is more convenient.
[350](https://docs.rs#350)        ///
[351](https://docs.rs#351)        /// ```
[352](https://docs.rs#352)        /// # use quote::quote;
[353](https://docs.rs#353)        /// #
[354](https://docs.rs#354)        /// # let field_type = quote!(...);
[355](https://docs.rs#355)        /// #
[356](https://docs.rs#356)        /// quote! {
[357](https://docs.rs#357)        ///     let value = <#field_type>::new();
[358](https://docs.rs#358)        /// }
[359](https://docs.rs#359)        /// # ;
[360](https://docs.rs#360)        /// ```
[361](https://docs.rs#361)        ///
[362](https://docs.rs#362)        /// This expands to `<Vec<i32>>::new()` which behaves correctly.
[363](https://docs.rs#363)        ///
[364](https://docs.rs#364)        /// A similar pattern is appropriate for trait methods.
[365](https://docs.rs#365)        ///
[366](https://docs.rs#366)        /// ```
[367](https://docs.rs#367)        /// # use quote::quote;
[368](https://docs.rs#368)        /// #
[369](https://docs.rs#369)        /// # let field_type = quote!(...);
[370](https://docs.rs#370)        /// #
[371](https://docs.rs#371)        /// quote! {
[372](https://docs.rs#372)        ///     let value = <#field_type as core::default::Default>::default();
[373](https://docs.rs#373)        /// }
[374](https://docs.rs#374)        /// # ;
[375](https://docs.rs#375)        /// ```
[376](https://docs.rs#376)        ///
[377](https://docs.rs#377)        /// <p><br></p>
[378](https://docs.rs#378)        ///
[379](https://docs.rs#379)        /// ### Interpolating text inside of doc comments
[380](https://docs.rs#380)        ///
[381](https://docs.rs#381)        /// Neither doc comments nor string literals get interpolation behavior in
[382](https://docs.rs#382)        /// quote:
[383](https://docs.rs#383)        ///
[384](https://docs.rs#384)        /// ```compile_fail
[385](https://docs.rs#385)        /// quote! {
[386](https://docs.rs#386)        ///     /// try to interpolate: #ident
[387](https://docs.rs#387)        ///     ///
[388](https://docs.rs#388)        ///     /// ...
[389](https://docs.rs#389)        /// }
[390](https://docs.rs#390)        /// ```
[391](https://docs.rs#391)        ///
[392](https://docs.rs#392)        /// ```compile_fail
[393](https://docs.rs#393)        /// quote! {
[394](https://docs.rs#394)        ///     #[doc = "try to interpolate: #ident"]
[395](https://docs.rs#395)        /// }
[396](https://docs.rs#396)        /// ```
[397](https://docs.rs#397)        ///
[398](https://docs.rs#398)        /// Instead the best way to build doc comments that involve variables is by
[399](https://docs.rs#399)        /// formatting the doc string literal outside of quote.
[400](https://docs.rs#400)        ///
[401](https://docs.rs#401)        /// ```rust
[402](https://docs.rs#402)        /// # use proc_macro2::{Ident, Span};
[403](https://docs.rs#403)        /// # use quote::quote;
[404](https://docs.rs#404)        /// #
[405](https://docs.rs#405)        /// # const IGNORE: &str = stringify! {
[406](https://docs.rs#406)        /// let msg = format!(...);
[407](https://docs.rs#407)        /// # };
[408](https://docs.rs#408)        /// #
[409](https://docs.rs#409)        /// # let ident = Ident::new("var", Span::call_site());
[410](https://docs.rs#410)        /// # let msg = format!("try to interpolate: {}", ident);
[411](https://docs.rs#411)        /// quote! {
[412](https://docs.rs#412)        ///     #[doc = #msg]
[413](https://docs.rs#413)        ///     ///
[414](https://docs.rs#414)        ///     /// ...
[415](https://docs.rs#415)        /// }
[416](https://docs.rs#416)        /// # ;
[417](https://docs.rs#417)        /// ```
[418](https://docs.rs#418)        ///
[419](https://docs.rs#419)        /// <p><br></p>
[420](https://docs.rs#420)        ///
[421](https://docs.rs#421)        /// ### Indexing into a tuple struct
[422](https://docs.rs#422)        ///
[423](https://docs.rs#423)        /// When interpolating indices of a tuple or tuple struct, we need them not to
[424](https://docs.rs#424)        /// appears suffixed as integer literals by interpolating them as [`syn::Index`]
[425](https://docs.rs#425)        /// instead.
[426](https://docs.rs#426)        ///
[427](https://docs.rs#427)        /// [`syn::Index`]: https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/struct.Index.html
[428](https://docs.rs#428)        ///
[429](https://docs.rs#429)        /// ```compile_fail
[430](https://docs.rs#430)        /// let i = 0usize..self.fields.len();
[431](https://docs.rs#431)        ///
[432](https://docs.rs#432)        /// // expands to 0 + self.0usize.heap_size() + self.1usize.heap_size() + ...
[433](https://docs.rs#433)        /// // which is not valid syntax
[434](https://docs.rs#434)        /// quote! {
[435](https://docs.rs#435)        ///     0 #( + self.#i.heap_size() )*
[436](https://docs.rs#436)        /// }
[437](https://docs.rs#437)        /// ```
[438](https://docs.rs#438)        ///
[439](https://docs.rs#439)        /// ```
[440](https://docs.rs#440)        /// # use proc_macro2::{Ident, TokenStream};
[441](https://docs.rs#441)        /// # use quote::quote;
[442](https://docs.rs#442)        /// #
[443](https://docs.rs#443)        /// # mod syn {
[444](https://docs.rs#444)        /// #     use proc_macro2::{Literal, TokenStream};
[445](https://docs.rs#445)        /// #     use quote::{ToTokens, TokenStreamExt};
[446](https://docs.rs#446)        /// #
[447](https://docs.rs#447)        /// #     pub struct Index(usize);
[448](https://docs.rs#448)        /// #
[449](https://docs.rs#449)        /// #     impl From<usize> for Index {
[450](https://docs.rs#450)        /// #         fn from(i: usize) -> Self {
[451](https://docs.rs#451)        /// #             Index(i)
[452](https://docs.rs#452)        /// #         }
[453](https://docs.rs#453)        /// #     }
[454](https://docs.rs#454)        /// #
[455](https://docs.rs#455)        /// #     impl ToTokens for Index {
[456](https://docs.rs#456)        /// #         fn to_tokens(&self, tokens: &mut TokenStream) {
[457](https://docs.rs#457)        /// #             tokens.append(Literal::usize_unsuffixed(self.0));
[458](https://docs.rs#458)        /// #         }
[459](https://docs.rs#459)        /// #     }
[460](https://docs.rs#460)        /// # }
[461](https://docs.rs#461)        /// #
[462](https://docs.rs#462)        /// # struct Struct {
[463](https://docs.rs#463)        /// #     fields: Vec<Ident>,
[464](https://docs.rs#464)        /// # }
[465](https://docs.rs#465)        /// #
[466](https://docs.rs#466)        /// # impl Struct {
[467](https://docs.rs#467)        /// #     fn example(&self) -> TokenStream {
[468](https://docs.rs#468)        /// let i = (0..self.fields.len()).map(syn::Index::from);
[469](https://docs.rs#469)        ///
[470](https://docs.rs#470)        /// // expands to 0 + self.0.heap_size() + self.1.heap_size() + ...
[471](https://docs.rs#471)        /// quote! {
[472](https://docs.rs#472)        ///     0 #( + self.#i.heap_size() )*
[473](https://docs.rs#473)        /// }
[474](https://docs.rs#474)        /// #     }
[475](https://docs.rs#475)        /// # }
[476](https://docs.rs#476)        /// ```
[477](https://docs.rs#477)        $quote
[478](https://docs.rs#478)    };
[479](https://docs.rs#479)}
[480](https://docs.rs#480)
[481](https://docs.rs#481)#[cfg(doc)]
[482](https://docs.rs#482)__quote![
[483](https://docs.rs#483)    #[macro_export]
[484](https://docs.rs#484)    macro_rules! [quote](https://docs.rs/quote/macro.quote.html) {
[485](https://docs.rs#485)        ($($tt:tt)*) => {
[486](https://docs.rs#486)            ...
[487](https://docs.rs#487)        };
[488](https://docs.rs#488)    }
[489](https://docs.rs#489)];
[490](https://docs.rs#490)
[491](https://docs.rs#491)#[cfg(not(doc))]
[492](https://docs.rs#492)__quote![
[493](https://docs.rs#493)    #[macro_export]
[494](https://docs.rs#494)    macro_rules! quote {
[495](https://docs.rs#495)        () => {
[496](https://docs.rs#496)            $crate::__private::TokenStream::new()
[497](https://docs.rs#497)        };
[498](https://docs.rs#498)
[499](https://docs.rs#499)        // Special case rule for a single tt, for performance.
[500](https://docs.rs#500)        ($tt:tt) => {{
[501](https://docs.rs#501)            let mut _s = $crate::__private::TokenStream::new();
[502](https://docs.rs#502)            $crate::quote_token!{$tt _s}
[503](https://docs.rs#503)            _s
[504](https://docs.rs#504)        }};
[505](https://docs.rs#505)
[506](https://docs.rs#506)        // Special case rules for two tts, for performance.
[507](https://docs.rs#507)        (# $var:ident) => {{
[508](https://docs.rs#508)            let mut _s = $crate::__private::TokenStream::new();
[509](https://docs.rs#509)            $crate::ToTokens::to_tokens(&$var, &mut _s);
[510](https://docs.rs#510)            _s
[511](https://docs.rs#511)        }};
[512](https://docs.rs#512)        ($tt1:tt $tt2:tt) => {{
[513](https://docs.rs#513)            let mut _s = $crate::__private::TokenStream::new();
[514](https://docs.rs#514)            $crate::quote_token!{$tt1 _s}
[515](https://docs.rs#515)            $crate::quote_token!{$tt2 _s}
[516](https://docs.rs#516)            _s
[517](https://docs.rs#517)        }};
[518](https://docs.rs#518)
[519](https://docs.rs#519)        // Rule for any other number of tokens.
[520](https://docs.rs#520)        ($($tt:tt)*) => {{
[521](https://docs.rs#521)            let mut _s = $crate::__private::TokenStream::new();
[522](https://docs.rs#522)            $crate::quote_each_token!{_s $($tt)*}
[523](https://docs.rs#523)            _s
[524](https://docs.rs#524)        }};
[525](https://docs.rs#525)    }
[526](https://docs.rs#526)];
[527](https://docs.rs#527)
[528](https://docs.rs#528)/// Same as `quote!`, but applies a given span to all tokens originating within
[529](https://docs.rs#529)/// the macro invocation.
[530](https://docs.rs#530)///
[531](https://docs.rs#531)/// <br>
[532](https://docs.rs#532)///
[533](https://docs.rs#533)/// # Syntax
[534](https://docs.rs#534)///
[535](https://docs.rs#535)/// A span expression of type [`Span`], followed by `=>`, followed by the tokens
[536](https://docs.rs#536)/// to quote. The span expression should be brief — use a variable for
[537](https://docs.rs#537)/// anything more than a few characters. There should be no space before the
[538](https://docs.rs#538)/// `=>` token.
[539](https://docs.rs#539)///
[540](https://docs.rs#540)/// [`Span`]: proc_macro2::Span
[541](https://docs.rs#541)///
[542](https://docs.rs#542)/// ```
[543](https://docs.rs#543)/// # use proc_macro2::Span;
[544](https://docs.rs#544)/// # use quote::quote_spanned;
[545](https://docs.rs#545)/// #
[546](https://docs.rs#546)/// # const IGNORE_TOKENS: &'static str = stringify! {
[547](https://docs.rs#547)/// let span = /* ... */;
[548](https://docs.rs#548)/// # };
[549](https://docs.rs#549)/// # let span = Span::call_site();
[550](https://docs.rs#550)/// # let init = 0;
[551](https://docs.rs#551)///
[552](https://docs.rs#552)/// // On one line, use parentheses.
[553](https://docs.rs#553)/// let tokens = quote_spanned!(span=> Box::into_raw(Box::new(#init)));
[554](https://docs.rs#554)///
[555](https://docs.rs#555)/// // On multiple lines, place the span at the top and use braces.
[556](https://docs.rs#556)/// let tokens = quote_spanned! {span=>
[557](https://docs.rs#557)///     Box::into_raw(Box::new(#init))
[558](https://docs.rs#558)/// };
[559](https://docs.rs#559)/// ```
[560](https://docs.rs#560)///
[561](https://docs.rs#561)/// The lack of space before the `=>` should look jarring to Rust programmers
[562](https://docs.rs#562)/// and this is intentional. The formatting is designed to be visibly
[563](https://docs.rs#563)/// off-balance and draw the eye a particular way, due to the span expression
[564](https://docs.rs#564)/// being evaluated in the context of the procedural macro and the remaining
[565](https://docs.rs#565)/// tokens being evaluated in the generated code.
[566](https://docs.rs#566)///
[567](https://docs.rs#567)/// <br>
[568](https://docs.rs#568)///
[569](https://docs.rs#569)/// # Hygiene
[570](https://docs.rs#570)///
[571](https://docs.rs#571)/// Any interpolated tokens preserve the `Span` information provided by their
[572](https://docs.rs#572)/// `ToTokens` implementation. Tokens that originate within the `quote_spanned!`
[573](https://docs.rs#573)/// invocation are spanned with the given span argument.
[574](https://docs.rs#574)///
[575](https://docs.rs#575)/// <br>
[576](https://docs.rs#576)///
[577](https://docs.rs#577)/// # Example
[578](https://docs.rs#578)///
[579](https://docs.rs#579)/// The following procedural macro code uses `quote_spanned!` to assert that a
[580](https://docs.rs#580)/// particular Rust type implements the [`Sync`] trait so that references can be
[581](https://docs.rs#581)/// safely shared between threads.
[582](https://docs.rs#582)///
[583](https://docs.rs#583)/// ```
[584](https://docs.rs#584)/// # use quote::{quote_spanned, TokenStreamExt, ToTokens};
[585](https://docs.rs#585)/// # use proc_macro2::{Span, TokenStream};
[586](https://docs.rs#586)/// #
[587](https://docs.rs#587)/// # struct Type;
[588](https://docs.rs#588)/// #
[589](https://docs.rs#589)/// # impl Type {
[590](https://docs.rs#590)/// #     fn span(&self) -> Span {
[591](https://docs.rs#591)/// #         Span::call_site()
[592](https://docs.rs#592)/// #     }
[593](https://docs.rs#593)/// # }
[594](https://docs.rs#594)/// #
[595](https://docs.rs#595)/// # impl ToTokens for Type {
[596](https://docs.rs#596)/// #     fn to_tokens(&self, _tokens: &mut TokenStream) {}
[597](https://docs.rs#597)/// # }
[598](https://docs.rs#598)/// #
[599](https://docs.rs#599)/// # let ty = Type;
[600](https://docs.rs#600)/// # let call_site = Span::call_site();
[601](https://docs.rs#601)/// #
[602](https://docs.rs#602)/// let ty_span = ty.span();
[603](https://docs.rs#603)/// let assert_sync = quote_spanned! {ty_span=>
[604](https://docs.rs#604)///     struct _AssertSync where #ty: Sync;
[605](https://docs.rs#605)/// };
[606](https://docs.rs#606)/// ```
[607](https://docs.rs#607)///
[608](https://docs.rs#608)/// If the assertion fails, the user will see an error like the following. The
[609](https://docs.rs#609)/// input span of their type is highlighted in the error.
[610](https://docs.rs#610)///
[611](https://docs.rs#611)/// ```text
[612](https://docs.rs#612)/// error[E0277]: the trait bound `*const (): std::marker::Sync` is not satisfied
[613](https://docs.rs#613)///   --> src/main.rs:10:21
[614](https://docs.rs#614)///    |
[615](https://docs.rs#615)/// 10 |     static ref PTR: *const () = &();
[616](https://docs.rs#616)///    |                     ^^^^^^^^^ `*const ()` cannot be shared between threads safely
[617](https://docs.rs#617)/// ```
[618](https://docs.rs#618)///
[619](https://docs.rs#619)/// In this example it is important for the where-clause to be spanned with the
[620](https://docs.rs#620)/// line/column information of the user's input type so that error messages are
[621](https://docs.rs#621)/// placed appropriately by the compiler.
[622](https://docs.rs#622)#[macro_export]
[623](https://docs.rs#623)macro_rules! [quote_spanned](https://docs.rs/quote/macro.quote_spanned.html) {
[624](https://docs.rs#624)    ($span:expr=> $($tt:tt)*) => {{
[625](https://docs.rs#625)        let _span: $crate::__private::Span = $crate::__private::get_span($span).__into_span();
[626](https://docs.rs#626)        $crate::quote_spanned_with_expanded_span!{_span $($tt)*}
[627](https://docs.rs#627)    }};
[628](https://docs.rs#628)}
[629](https://docs.rs#629)
[630](https://docs.rs#630)// We want to ensure that `get_span` only gets called for the actual user
[631](https://docs.rs#631)// invocation and not for recursive calls from groups, which will call this
[632](https://docs.rs#632)// inner macro instead.
[633](https://docs.rs#633)#[macro_export]
[634](https://docs.rs#634)#[doc(hidden)]
[635](https://docs.rs#635)macro_rules! quote_spanned_with_expanded_span {
[636](https://docs.rs#636)    ($span:ident) => {
[637](https://docs.rs#637)        $crate::__private::TokenStream::new()
[638](https://docs.rs#638)    };
[639](https://docs.rs#639)
[640](https://docs.rs#640)    // Special case rule for a single tt, for performance.
[641](https://docs.rs#641)    ($span:ident $tt:tt) => {
[642](https://docs.rs#642)        let mut _s = $crate::__private::TokenStream::new();
[643](https://docs.rs#643)        $crate::quote_token_spanned!{$tt _s $span}
[644](https://docs.rs#644)        _s
[645](https://docs.rs#645)    };
[646](https://docs.rs#646)
[647](https://docs.rs#647)    // Special case rules for two tts, for performance.
[648](https://docs.rs#648)    ($span:ident # $var:ident) => {
[649](https://docs.rs#649)        let mut _s = $crate::__private::TokenStream::new();
[650](https://docs.rs#650)        $crate::ToTokens::to_tokens(&$var, &mut _s);
[651](https://docs.rs#651)        _s
[652](https://docs.rs#652)    };
[653](https://docs.rs#653)    ($span:ident $tt1:tt $tt2:tt) => {
[654](https://docs.rs#654)        let mut _s = $crate::__private::TokenStream::new();
[655](https://docs.rs#655)        $crate::quote_token_spanned!{$tt1 _s $span}
[656](https://docs.rs#656)        $crate::quote_token_spanned!{$tt2 _s $span}
[657](https://docs.rs#657)        _s
[658](https://docs.rs#658)    };
[659](https://docs.rs#659)
[660](https://docs.rs#660)    // Rule for any other number of tokens.
[661](https://docs.rs#661)    ($span:ident $($tt:tt)*) => {
[662](https://docs.rs#662)        let mut _s = $crate::__private::TokenStream::new();
[663](https://docs.rs#663)        $crate::quote_each_token_spanned!{_s $span $($tt)*}
[664](https://docs.rs#664)        _s
[665](https://docs.rs#665)    };
[666](https://docs.rs#666)}
[667](https://docs.rs#667)
[668](https://docs.rs#668)// Extract the names of all #metavariables and pass them to the $call macro.
[669](https://docs.rs#669)//
[670](https://docs.rs#670)// in:   pounded_var_names!(then!(...) a #b c #( #d )* #e)
[671](https://docs.rs#671)// out:  then!(... b);
[672](https://docs.rs#672)//       then!(... d);
[673](https://docs.rs#673)//       then!(... e);
[674](https://docs.rs#674)#[macro_export]
[675](https://docs.rs#675)#[doc(hidden)]
[676](https://docs.rs#676)macro_rules! pounded_var_names {
[677](https://docs.rs#677)    ($call:ident! $extra:tt $($tts:tt)*) => {
[678](https://docs.rs#678)        $crate::pounded_var_names_with_context!{$call! $extra
[679](https://docs.rs#679)            (@ $($tts)*)
[680](https://docs.rs#680)            ($($tts)* @)
[681](https://docs.rs#681)        }
[682](https://docs.rs#682)    };
[683](https://docs.rs#683)}
[684](https://docs.rs#684)
[685](https://docs.rs#685)#[macro_export]
[686](https://docs.rs#686)#[doc(hidden)]
[687](https://docs.rs#687)macro_rules! pounded_var_names_with_context {
[688](https://docs.rs#688)    ($call:ident! $extra:tt ($($b1:tt)*) ($($curr:tt)*)) => {
[689](https://docs.rs#689)        $(
[690](https://docs.rs#690)            $crate::pounded_var_with_context!{$call! $extra $b1 $curr}
[691](https://docs.rs#691)        )*
[692](https://docs.rs#692)    };
[693](https://docs.rs#693)}
[694](https://docs.rs#694)
[695](https://docs.rs#695)#[macro_export]
[696](https://docs.rs#696)#[doc(hidden)]
[697](https://docs.rs#697)macro_rules! pounded_var_with_context {
[698](https://docs.rs#698)    ($call:ident! $extra:tt $b1:tt ( $($inner:tt)* )) => {
[699](https://docs.rs#699)        $crate::pounded_var_names!{$call! $extra $($inner)*}
[700](https://docs.rs#700)    };
[701](https://docs.rs#701)
[702](https://docs.rs#702)    ($call:ident! $extra:tt $b1:tt [ $($inner:tt)* ]) => {
[703](https://docs.rs#703)        $crate::pounded_var_names!{$call! $extra $($inner)*}
[704](https://docs.rs#704)    };
[705](https://docs.rs#705)
[706](https://docs.rs#706)    ($call:ident! $extra:tt $b1:tt { $($inner:tt)* }) => {
[707](https://docs.rs#707)        $crate::pounded_var_names!{$call! $extra $($inner)*}
[708](https://docs.rs#708)    };
[709](https://docs.rs#709)
[710](https://docs.rs#710)    ($call:ident!($($extra:tt)*) # $var:ident) => {
[711](https://docs.rs#711)        $crate::$call!($($extra)* $var);
[712](https://docs.rs#712)    };
[713](https://docs.rs#713)
[714](https://docs.rs#714)    ($call:ident! $extra:tt $b1:tt $curr:tt) => {};
[715](https://docs.rs#715)}
[716](https://docs.rs#716)
[717](https://docs.rs#717)#[macro_export]
[718](https://docs.rs#718)#[doc(hidden)]
[719](https://docs.rs#719)macro_rules! quote_bind_into_iter {
[720](https://docs.rs#720)    ($has_iter:ident $var:ident) => {
[721](https://docs.rs#721)        // `mut` may be unused if $var occurs multiple times in the list.
[722](https://docs.rs#722)        #[allow(unused_mut)]
[723](https://docs.rs#723)        let (mut $var, i) = $var.quote_into_iter();
[724](https://docs.rs#724)        let $has_iter = $has_iter | i;
[725](https://docs.rs#725)    };
[726](https://docs.rs#726)}
[727](https://docs.rs#727)
[728](https://docs.rs#728)#[macro_export]
[729](https://docs.rs#729)#[doc(hidden)]
[730](https://docs.rs#730)macro_rules! quote_bind_next_or_break {
[731](https://docs.rs#731)    ($var:ident) => {
[732](https://docs.rs#732)        let $var = match $var.next() {
[733](https://docs.rs#733)            Some(_x) => $crate::__private::RepInterp(_x),
[734](https://docs.rs#734)            None => break,
[735](https://docs.rs#735)        };
[736](https://docs.rs#736)    };
[737](https://docs.rs#737)}
[738](https://docs.rs#738)
[739](https://docs.rs#739)// The obvious way to write this macro is as a tt muncher. This implementation
[740](https://docs.rs#740)// does something more complex for two reasons.
[741](https://docs.rs#741)//
[742](https://docs.rs#742)//   - With a tt muncher it's easy to hit Rust's built-in recursion_limit, which
[743](https://docs.rs#743)//     this implementation avoids because it isn't tail recursive.
[744](https://docs.rs#744)//
[745](https://docs.rs#745)//   - Compile times for a tt muncher are quadratic relative to the length of
[746](https://docs.rs#746)//     the input. This implementation is linear, so it will be faster
[747](https://docs.rs#747)//     (potentially much faster) for big inputs. However, the constant factors
[748](https://docs.rs#748)//     of this implementation are higher than that of a tt muncher, so it is
[749](https://docs.rs#749)//     somewhat slower than a tt muncher if there are many invocations with
[750](https://docs.rs#750)//     short inputs.
[751](https://docs.rs#751)//
[752](https://docs.rs#752)// An invocation like this:
[753](https://docs.rs#753)//
[754](https://docs.rs#754)//     quote_each_token!(_s a b c d e f g h i j);
[755](https://docs.rs#755)//
[756](https://docs.rs#756)// expands to this:
[757](https://docs.rs#757)//
[758](https://docs.rs#758)//     quote_tokens_with_context!(_s
[759](https://docs.rs#759)//         (@  @  @  @   @   @   a   b   c   d   e   f   g  h  i  j)
[760](https://docs.rs#760)//         (@  @  @  @   @   a   b   c   d   e   f   g   h  i  j  @)
[761](https://docs.rs#761)//         (@  @  @  @   a   b   c   d   e   f   g   h   i  j  @  @)
[762](https://docs.rs#762)//         (@  @  @ (a) (b) (c) (d) (e) (f) (g) (h) (i) (j) @  @  @)
[763](https://docs.rs#763)//         (@  @  a  b   c   d   e   f   g   h   i   j   @  @  @  @)
[764](https://docs.rs#764)//         (@  a  b  c   d   e   f   g   h   i   j   @   @  @  @  @)
[765](https://docs.rs#765)//         (a  b  c  d   e   f   g   h   i   j   @   @   @  @  @  @)
[766](https://docs.rs#766)//     );
[767](https://docs.rs#767)//
[768](https://docs.rs#768)// which gets transposed and expanded to this:
[769](https://docs.rs#769)//
[770](https://docs.rs#770)//     quote_token_with_context!(_s @ @ @  @  @ @ a);
[771](https://docs.rs#771)//     quote_token_with_context!(_s @ @ @  @  @ a b);
[772](https://docs.rs#772)//     quote_token_with_context!(_s @ @ @  @  a b c);
[773](https://docs.rs#773)//     quote_token_with_context!(_s @ @ @ (a) b c d);
[774](https://docs.rs#774)//     quote_token_with_context!(_s @ @ a (b) c d e);
[775](https://docs.rs#775)//     quote_token_with_context!(_s @ a b (c) d e f);
[776](https://docs.rs#776)//     quote_token_with_context!(_s a b c (d) e f g);
[777](https://docs.rs#777)//     quote_token_with_context!(_s b c d (e) f g h);
[778](https://docs.rs#778)//     quote_token_with_context!(_s c d e (f) g h i);
[779](https://docs.rs#779)//     quote_token_with_context!(_s d e f (g) h i j);
[780](https://docs.rs#780)//     quote_token_with_context!(_s e f g (h) i j @);
[781](https://docs.rs#781)//     quote_token_with_context!(_s f g h (i) j @ @);
[782](https://docs.rs#782)//     quote_token_with_context!(_s g h i (j) @ @ @);
[783](https://docs.rs#783)//     quote_token_with_context!(_s h i j  @  @ @ @);
[784](https://docs.rs#784)//     quote_token_with_context!(_s i j @  @  @ @ @);
[785](https://docs.rs#785)//     quote_token_with_context!(_s j @ @  @  @ @ @);
[786](https://docs.rs#786)//
[787](https://docs.rs#787)// Without having used muncher-style recursion, we get one invocation of
[788](https://docs.rs#788)// quote_token_with_context for each original tt, with three tts of context on
[789](https://docs.rs#789)// either side. This is enough for the longest possible interpolation form (a
[790](https://docs.rs#790)// repetition with separator, as in `# (#var) , *`) to be fully represented with
[791](https://docs.rs#791)// the first or last tt in the middle.
[792](https://docs.rs#792)//
[793](https://docs.rs#793)// The middle tt (surrounded by parentheses) is the tt being processed.
[794](https://docs.rs#794)//
[795](https://docs.rs#795)//   - When it is a `#`, quote_token_with_context can do an interpolation. The
[796](https://docs.rs#796)//     interpolation kind will depend on the three subsequent tts.
[797](https://docs.rs#797)//
[798](https://docs.rs#798)//   - When it is within a later part of an interpolation, it can be ignored
[799](https://docs.rs#799)//     because the interpolation has already been done.
[800](https://docs.rs#800)//
[801](https://docs.rs#801)//   - When it is not part of an interpolation it can be pushed as a single
[802](https://docs.rs#802)//     token into the output.
[803](https://docs.rs#803)//
[804](https://docs.rs#804)//   - When the middle token is an unparenthesized `@`, that call is one of the
[805](https://docs.rs#805)//     first 3 or last 3 calls of quote_token_with_context and does not
[806](https://docs.rs#806)//     correspond to one of the original input tokens, so turns into nothing.
[807](https://docs.rs#807)#[macro_export]
[808](https://docs.rs#808)#[doc(hidden)]
[809](https://docs.rs#809)macro_rules! quote_each_token {
[810](https://docs.rs#810)    ($tokens:ident $($tts:tt)*) => {
[811](https://docs.rs#811)        $crate::quote_tokens_with_context!{$tokens
[812](https://docs.rs#812)            (@ @ @ @ @ @ $($tts)*)
[813](https://docs.rs#813)            (@ @ @ @ @ $($tts)* @)
[814](https://docs.rs#814)            (@ @ @ @ $($tts)* @ @)
[815](https://docs.rs#815)            (@ @ @ $(($tts))* @ @ @)
[816](https://docs.rs#816)            (@ @ $($tts)* @ @ @ @)
[817](https://docs.rs#817)            (@ $($tts)* @ @ @ @ @)
[818](https://docs.rs#818)            ($($tts)* @ @ @ @ @ @)
[819](https://docs.rs#819)        }
[820](https://docs.rs#820)    };
[821](https://docs.rs#821)}
[822](https://docs.rs#822)
[823](https://docs.rs#823)// See the explanation on quote_each_token.
[824](https://docs.rs#824)#[macro_export]
[825](https://docs.rs#825)#[doc(hidden)]
[826](https://docs.rs#826)macro_rules! quote_each_token_spanned {
[827](https://docs.rs#827)    ($tokens:ident $span:ident $($tts:tt)*) => {
[828](https://docs.rs#828)        $crate::quote_tokens_with_context_spanned!{$tokens $span
[829](https://docs.rs#829)            (@ @ @ @ @ @ $($tts)*)
[830](https://docs.rs#830)            (@ @ @ @ @ $($tts)* @)
[831](https://docs.rs#831)            (@ @ @ @ $($tts)* @ @)
[832](https://docs.rs#832)            (@ @ @ $(($tts))* @ @ @)
[833](https://docs.rs#833)            (@ @ $($tts)* @ @ @ @)
[834](https://docs.rs#834)            (@ $($tts)* @ @ @ @ @)
[835](https://docs.rs#835)            ($($tts)* @ @ @ @ @ @)
[836](https://docs.rs#836)        }
[837](https://docs.rs#837)    };
[838](https://docs.rs#838)}
[839](https://docs.rs#839)
[840](https://docs.rs#840)// See the explanation on quote_each_token.
[841](https://docs.rs#841)#[macro_export]
[842](https://docs.rs#842)#[doc(hidden)]
[843](https://docs.rs#843)macro_rules! quote_tokens_with_context {
[844](https://docs.rs#844)    ($tokens:ident
[845](https://docs.rs#845)        ($($b3:tt)*) ($($b2:tt)*) ($($b1:tt)*)
[846](https://docs.rs#846)        ($($curr:tt)*)
[847](https://docs.rs#847)        ($($a1:tt)*) ($($a2:tt)*) ($($a3:tt)*)
[848](https://docs.rs#848)    ) => {
[849](https://docs.rs#849)        $(
[850](https://docs.rs#850)            $crate::quote_token_with_context!{$tokens $b3 $b2 $b1 $curr $a1 $a2 $a3}
[851](https://docs.rs#851)        )*
[852](https://docs.rs#852)    };
[853](https://docs.rs#853)}
[854](https://docs.rs#854)
[855](https://docs.rs#855)// See the explanation on quote_each_token.
[856](https://docs.rs#856)#[macro_export]
[857](https://docs.rs#857)#[doc(hidden)]
[858](https://docs.rs#858)macro_rules! quote_tokens_with_context_spanned {
[859](https://docs.rs#859)    ($tokens:ident $span:ident
[860](https://docs.rs#860)        ($($b3:tt)*) ($($b2:tt)*) ($($b1:tt)*)
[861](https://docs.rs#861)        ($($curr:tt)*)
[862](https://docs.rs#862)        ($($a1:tt)*) ($($a2:tt)*) ($($a3:tt)*)
[863](https://docs.rs#863)    ) => {
[864](https://docs.rs#864)        $(
[865](https://docs.rs#865)            $crate::quote_token_with_context_spanned!{$tokens $span $b3 $b2 $b1 $curr $a1 $a2 $a3}
[866](https://docs.rs#866)        )*
[867](https://docs.rs#867)    };
[868](https://docs.rs#868)}
[869](https://docs.rs#869)
[870](https://docs.rs#870)// See the explanation on quote_each_token.
[871](https://docs.rs#871)#[macro_export]
[872](https://docs.rs#872)#[doc(hidden)]
[873](https://docs.rs#873)macro_rules! quote_token_with_context {
[874](https://docs.rs#874)    // Unparenthesized `@` indicates this call does not correspond to one of the
[875](https://docs.rs#875)    // original input tokens. Ignore it.
[876](https://docs.rs#876)    ($tokens:ident $b3:tt $b2:tt $b1:tt @ $a1:tt $a2:tt $a3:tt) => {};
[877](https://docs.rs#877)
[878](https://docs.rs#878)    // A repetition with no separator.
[879](https://docs.rs#879)    ($tokens:ident $b3:tt $b2:tt $b1:tt (#) ( $($inner:tt)* ) * $a3:tt) => {{
[880](https://docs.rs#880)        use $crate::__private::ext::*;
[881](https://docs.rs#881)        let has_iter = $crate::__private::HasIterator::<false>;
[882](https://docs.rs#882)        $crate::pounded_var_names!{quote_bind_into_iter!(has_iter) () $($inner)*}
[883](https://docs.rs#883)        <_ as $crate::__private::CheckHasIterator<true>>::check(has_iter);
[884](https://docs.rs#884)        // This is `while true` instead of `loop` because if there are no
[885](https://docs.rs#885)        // iterators used inside of this repetition then the body would not
[886](https://docs.rs#886)        // contain any `break`, so the compiler would emit unreachable code
[887](https://docs.rs#887)        // warnings on anything below the loop. We use has_iter to detect and
[888](https://docs.rs#888)        // fail to compile when there are no iterators, so here we just work
[889](https://docs.rs#889)        // around the unneeded extra warning.
[890](https://docs.rs#890)        while true {
[891](https://docs.rs#891)            $crate::pounded_var_names!{quote_bind_next_or_break!() () $($inner)*}
[892](https://docs.rs#892)            $crate::quote_each_token!{$tokens $($inner)*}
[893](https://docs.rs#893)        }
[894](https://docs.rs#894)    }};
[895](https://docs.rs#895)    // ... and one step later.
[896](https://docs.rs#896)    ($tokens:ident $b3:tt $b2:tt # (( $($inner:tt)* )) * $a2:tt $a3:tt) => {};
[897](https://docs.rs#897)    // ... and one step later.
[898](https://docs.rs#898)    ($tokens:ident $b3:tt # ( $($inner:tt)* ) (*) $a1:tt $a2:tt $a3:tt) => {};
[899](https://docs.rs#899)
[900](https://docs.rs#900)    // A repetition with separator.
[901](https://docs.rs#901)    ($tokens:ident $b3:tt $b2:tt $b1:tt (#) ( $($inner:tt)* ) $sep:tt *) => {{
[902](https://docs.rs#902)        use $crate::__private::ext::*;
[903](https://docs.rs#903)        let mut _first = true;
[904](https://docs.rs#904)        let has_iter = $crate::__private::HasIterator::<false>;
[905](https://docs.rs#905)        $crate::pounded_var_names!{quote_bind_into_iter!(has_iter) () $($inner)*}
[906](https://docs.rs#906)        <_ as $crate::__private::CheckHasIterator<true>>::check(has_iter);
[907](https://docs.rs#907)        while true {
[908](https://docs.rs#908)            $crate::pounded_var_names!{quote_bind_next_or_break!() () $($inner)*}
[909](https://docs.rs#909)            if !_first {
[910](https://docs.rs#910)                $crate::quote_token!{$sep $tokens}
[911](https://docs.rs#911)            }
[912](https://docs.rs#912)            _first = false;
[913](https://docs.rs#913)            $crate::quote_each_token!{$tokens $($inner)*}
[914](https://docs.rs#914)        }
[915](https://docs.rs#915)    }};
[916](https://docs.rs#916)    // ... and one step later.
[917](https://docs.rs#917)    ($tokens:ident $b3:tt $b2:tt # (( $($inner:tt)* )) $sep:tt * $a3:tt) => {};
[918](https://docs.rs#918)    // ... and one step later.
[919](https://docs.rs#919)    ($tokens:ident $b3:tt # ( $($inner:tt)* ) ($sep:tt) * $a2:tt $a3:tt) => {};
[920](https://docs.rs#920)    // (A special case for `#(var)**`, where the first `*` is treated as the
[921](https://docs.rs#921)    // repetition symbol and the second `*` is treated as an ordinary token.)
[922](https://docs.rs#922)    ($tokens:ident # ( $($inner:tt)* ) * (*) $a1:tt $a2:tt $a3:tt) => {
[923](https://docs.rs#923)        // https://github.com/dtolnay/quote/issues/130
[924](https://docs.rs#924)        $crate::quote_token!{* $tokens}
[925](https://docs.rs#925)    };
[926](https://docs.rs#926)    // ... and one step later.
[927](https://docs.rs#927)    ($tokens:ident # ( $($inner:tt)* ) $sep:tt (*) $a1:tt $a2:tt $a3:tt) => {};
[928](https://docs.rs#928)

[932](https://docs.rs#932)    };
[933](https://docs.rs#933)    // ... and one step later.
[934](https://docs.rs#934)    ($tokens:ident $b3:tt $b2:tt # ($var:ident) $a1:tt $a2:tt $a3:tt) => {};
[935](https://docs.rs#935)

[937](https://docs.rs#937)    ($tokens:ident $b3:tt $b2:tt $b1:tt ($curr:tt) $a1:tt $a2:tt $a3:tt) => {

[994](https://docs.rs#994)
[995](https://docs.rs#995)// These rules are ordered by approximate token frequency, at least for the
[996](https://docs.rs#996)// first 10 or so, to improve compile times. Having `ident` first is by far the
[997](https://docs.rs#997)// most important because it's typically 2-3x more common than the next most
[998](https://docs.rs#998)// common token.
[999](https://docs.rs#999)//
[1000](https://docs.rs#1000)// Separately, we put the token being matched in the very front so that failing
[1001](https://docs.rs#1001)// rules may fail to match as quickly as possible.
[1002](https://docs.rs#1002)#[macro_export]
[1003](https://docs.rs#1003)#[doc(hidden)]
[1004](https://docs.rs#1004)macro_rules! quote_token {
[1005](https://docs.rs#1005)    ($ident:ident $tokens:ident) => {
[1006](https://docs.rs#1006)        $crate::__private::push_ident(
[1007](https://docs.rs#1007)            &mut $tokens,
[1008](https://docs.rs#1008)            $crate::__private::stringify!($ident),
[1009](https://docs.rs#1009)        );
[1010](https://docs.rs#1010)    };
[1011](https://docs.rs#1011)
[1012](https://docs.rs#1012)    (:: $tokens:ident) => {
[1013](https://docs.rs#1013)        $crate::__private::push_colon2(&mut $tokens);
[1014](https://docs.rs#1014)    };
[1015](https://docs.rs#1015)
[1016](https://docs.rs#1016)    (( $($inner:tt)* ) $tokens:ident) => {
[1017](https://docs.rs#1017)        $crate::__private::push_group(

[1019](https://docs.rs#1019)            $crate::__private::Delimiter::Parenthesis,
[1020](https://docs.rs#1020)            $crate::quote!($($inner)*),
[1021](https://docs.rs#1021)        );
[1022](https://docs.rs#1022)    };
[1023](https://docs.rs#1023)

# quote in quote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quote/1.0.46/quote/macro.quote.html

```
macro_rules! quote {
    ($($tt:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

The whole point.

Performs variable interpolation against the input and produces it as
[ proc_macro2::TokenStream](https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0.106/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/proc_macro2/struct.TokenStream.html).

Note: for returning tokens to the compiler in a procedural macro, use
`.into()` on the result to convert to [ proc_macro::TokenStream](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/proc_macro/struct.TokenStream.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#interpolation)Interpolation

Variable interpolation is done with `#var` (similar to `$var` in
`macro_rules!` macros). This grabs the `var` variable that is currently in
scope and inserts it in that location in the output tokens. Any type
implementing the [ ToTokens](https://docs.rs/trait.ToTokens.html) trait can be interpolated. This includes most
Rust primitive types as well as most of the syntax tree types from the

[Syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn)crate.

Repetition is done using `#(...)*` or `#(...),*` again similar to
`macro_rules!`. This iterates through the elements of any variable
interpolated within the repetition and inserts a copy of the repetition body
for each one. The variables in an interpolation may be a `Vec`, slice,
`BTreeSet`, or any `Iterator`.

- `#(#var)*`— no separators
- `#(#var),*`— the character before the asterisk is used as a separator
- `#( struct #var; )*`— the repetition can contain other tokens
- `#( #k => println!("{}", #v), )*`— even multiple interpolations

[§](https://docs.rs#hygiene)Hygiene

Any interpolated tokens preserve the `Span` information provided by their
`ToTokens` implementation. Tokens that originate within the `quote!`
invocation are spanned with [ Span::call_site()](https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0.106/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/proc_macro2/struct.Span.html#method.call_site).

A different span can be provided through the [ quote_spanned!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html) macro.

[§](https://docs.rs#return-type)Return type

The macro evaluates to an expression of type `proc_macro2::TokenStream`.
Meanwhile Rust procedural macros are expected to return the type
`proc_macro::TokenStream`.

The difference between the two types is that `proc_macro` types are entirely
specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a
procedural macro, while `proc_macro2` types may exist anywhere including
tests and non-macro code like main.rs and build.rs. This is why even the
procedural macro ecosystem is largely built around `proc_macro2`, because
that ensures the libraries are unit testable and accessible in non-macro
contexts.

There is a [ From](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/convert/trait.From.html)-conversion in both directions so returning the output of

`quote!` from a procedural macro usually looks like `tokens.into()` or
`proc_macro::TokenStream::from(tokens)`.[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#procedural-macro)Procedural macro

The structure of a basic procedural macro is as follows. Refer to the [Syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn)
crate for further useful guidance on using `quote!` as part of a procedural
macro.

```
extern crate proc_macro;
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
#[proc_macro_derive(HeapSize)]
pub fn derive_heap_size(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse the input and figure out what implementation to generate...
    let name = /* ... */;
    let expr = /* ... */;
    let expanded = quote! {
        // The generated impl.
        impl heapsize::HeapSize for #name {
            fn heap_size_of_children(&self) -> usize {
                #expr
            }
        }
    };
    // Hand the output tokens back to the compiler.
    TokenStream::from(expanded)
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#combining-quoted-fragments)Combining quoted fragments

Usually you don’t end up constructing an entire final `TokenStream` in one
piece. Different parts may come from different helper functions. The tokens
produced by `quote!` themselves implement `ToTokens` and so can be
interpolated into later `quote!` invocations to build up a final result.

```
let type_definition = quote! {...};
let methods = quote! {...};
let tokens = quote! {
    #type_definition
    #methods
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#constructing-identifiers)Constructing identifiers

Suppose we have an identifier `ident` which came from somewhere in a macro
input and we need to modify it in some way for the macro output. Let’s
consider prepending the identifier with an underscore.

Simply interpolating the identifier next to an underscore will not have the
behavior of concatenating them. The underscore and the identifier will
continue to be two separate tokens as if you had written `_ x`.

The solution is to build a new identifier token with the correct value. As
this is such a common case, the [ format_ident!](https://docs.rs/macro.format_ident.html) macro provides a
convenient utility for doing so correctly.

```
let varname = format_ident!("_{}", ident);
quote! {
    let mut #varname = 0;
}
```
Alternatively, the APIs provided by Syn and proc-macro2 can be used to
directly build the identifier. This is roughly equivalent to the above, but
will not handle `ident` being a raw identifier.

```
let concatenated = format!("_{}", ident);
let varname = syn::Ident::new(&concatenated, ident.span());
quote! {
    let mut #varname = 0;
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#making-method-calls)Making method calls

Let’s say our macro requires some type specified in the macro input to have
a constructor called `new`. We have the type in a variable called
`field_type` of type `syn::Type` and want to invoke the constructor.

```
// incorrect
quote! {
    let value = #field_type::new();
}
```
This works only sometimes. If `field_type` is `String`, the expanded code
contains `String::new()` which is fine. But if `field_type` is something
like `Vec<i32>` then the expanded code is `Vec<i32>::new()` which is invalid
syntax. Ordinarily in handwritten Rust we would write `Vec::<i32>::new()`
but for macros often the following is more convenient.

```
quote! {
    let value = <#field_type>::new();
}
```
This expands to `<Vec<i32>>::new()` which behaves correctly.

A similar pattern is appropriate for trait methods.

```
quote! {
    let value = <#field_type as core::default::Default>::default();
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#interpolating-text-inside-of-doc-comments)Interpolating text inside of doc comments

Neither doc comments nor string literals get interpolation behavior in quote:

Instead the best way to build doc comments that involve variables is by formatting the doc string literal outside of quote.

```
let msg = format!(...);
quote! {
    #[doc = #msg]
    ///
    /// ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#indexing-into-a-tuple-struct)Indexing into a tuple struct

When interpolating indices of a tuple or tuple struct, we need them not to
appears suffixed as integer literals by interpolating them as [ syn::Index](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/struct.Index.html)
instead.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let i = 0usize..self.fields.len();
// expands to 0 + self.0usize.heap_size() + self.1usize.heap_size() + ...
// which is not valid syntax
quote! {
    0 #( + self.#i.heap_size() )*
}
```
```
let i = (0..self.fields.len()).map(syn::Index::from);
// expands to 0 + self.0.heap_size() + self.1.heap_size() + ...
quote! {
    0 #( + self.#i.heap_size() )*
}
```

---

# quote_spanned in quote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quote/1.0.46/quote/macro.quote_spanned.html

```
macro_rules! quote_spanned {
    ($span:expr=> $($tt:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Same as `quote!`, but applies a given span to all tokens originating within
the macro invocation.

[§](https://docs.rs#syntax)Syntax

A span expression of type [ Span](https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0.106/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/proc_macro2/struct.Span.html), followed by

`=>`, followed by the tokens
to quote. The span expression should be brief — use a variable for
anything more than a few characters. There should be no space before the
`=>` token.```
let span = /* ... */;
// On one line, use parentheses.
let tokens = quote_spanned!(span=> Box::into_raw(Box::new(#init)));
// On multiple lines, place the span at the top and use braces.
let tokens = quote_spanned! {span=>
    Box::into_raw(Box::new(#init))
};
```
The lack of space before the `=>` should look jarring to Rust programmers
and this is intentional. The formatting is designed to be visibly
off-balance and draw the eye a particular way, due to the span expression
being evaluated in the context of the procedural macro and the remaining
tokens being evaluated in the generated code.

[§](https://docs.rs#hygiene)Hygiene

Any interpolated tokens preserve the `Span` information provided by their
`ToTokens` implementation. Tokens that originate within the `quote_spanned!`
invocation are spanned with the given span argument.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following procedural macro code uses `quote_spanned!` to assert that a
particular Rust type implements the [ Sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/trait.Sync.html) trait so that references can be
safely shared between threads.

```
let ty_span = ty.span();
let assert_sync = quote_spanned! {ty_span=>
    struct _AssertSync where #ty: Sync;
};
```
If the assertion fails, the user will see an error like the following. The input span of their type is highlighted in the error.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `*const (): std::marker::Sync` is not satisfied
  --> src/main.rs:10:21
   |
10 |     static ref PTR: *const () = &();
   |                     ^^^^^^^^^ `*const ()` cannot be shared between threads safely
```
In this example it is important for the where-clause to be spanned with the line/column information of the user’s input type so that error messages are placed appropriately by the compiler.

---

# format_ident in quote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quote/1.0.46/quote/macro.format_ident.html

```
macro_rules! format_ident {
    ($fmt:expr) => { ... };
    ($fmt:expr, $($rest:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Formatting macro for constructing `Ident`s.

[§](https://docs.rs#syntax)Syntax

Syntax is copied from the [ format!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/alloc/macro.format.html) macro, supporting both
positional and named arguments.

Only a limited set of formatting traits are supported. The current mapping of format types to traits is:

- `{}`⇒- `IdentFragment`
- `{:o}`⇒- `Octal`
- `{:x}`⇒- `LowerHex`
- `{:X}`⇒- `UpperHex`
- `{:b}`⇒- `Binary`

See [ core::fmt](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/index.html) for more information.

[§](https://docs.rs#identfragment)IdentFragment

Unlike `format!`, this macro uses the [ IdentFragment](https://docs.rs/trait.IdentFragment.html) formatting trait by
default. This trait is like

`Display`, with a few differences:- `IdentFragment`is only implemented for a limited set of types, such as unsigned integers and strings.
- `Ident`- `r#`prefixes stripped, if present.

[§](https://docs.rs#hygiene)Hygiene

The [ Span](https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0.106/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/proc_macro2/struct.Span.html) of the first

`Ident` argument is used as the span of the final
identifier, falling back to [when no identifiers are provided.](https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0.106/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/proc_macro2/struct.Span.html#method.call_site)

`Span::call_site````
// If `ident` is an Ident, the span of `my_ident` will be inherited from it.
let my_ident = format_ident!("My{}{}", ident, "IsCool");
assert_eq!(my_ident, "MyIdentIsCool");
```
Alternatively, the span can be overridden by passing the `span` named
argument.

```
let my_span = /* ... */;
format_ident!("MyIdent", span = my_span);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

This method will panic if the resulting formatted string is not a valid identifier.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Composing raw and non-raw identifiers:

```
let my_ident = format_ident!("My{}", "Ident");
assert_eq!(my_ident, "MyIdent");
let raw = format_ident!("r#Raw");
assert_eq!(raw, "r#Raw");
let my_ident_raw = format_ident!("{}Is{}", my_ident, raw);
assert_eq!(my_ident_raw, "MyIdentIsRaw");
```
Integer formatting options:

```
let num: u32 = 10;
let decimal = format_ident!("Id_{}", num);
assert_eq!(decimal, "Id_10");
let octal = format_ident!("Id_{:o}", num);
assert_eq!(octal, "Id_12");
let binary = format_ident!("Id_{:b}", num);
assert_eq!(binary, "Id_1010");
let lower_hex = format_ident!("Id_{:x}", num);
assert_eq!(lower_hex, "Id_a");
let upper_hex = format_ident!("Id_{:X}", num);
assert_eq!(upper_hex, "Id_A");
```

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/quote/to_tokens.rs.html#54)#### fn [to_tokens](https://docs.rs#tymethod.to_tokens)(&self, tokens: &mut [TokenStream](https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0.106/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/proc_macro2/struct.TokenStream.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/quote/to_tokens.rs.html#54)

#### fn [to_tokens](https://docs.rs#tymethod.to_tokens)(&self, tokens: &mut [TokenStream](https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0.106/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/proc_macro2/struct.TokenStream.html))

Write `self` to the given `TokenStream`.

The token append methods provided by the [ TokenStreamExt](https://docs.rs/trait.TokenStreamExt.html) extension
trait may be useful for implementing

`ToTokens`.[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Example implementation for a struct representing Rust paths like
`std::cmp::PartialEq`:

```
use proc_macro2::{TokenTree, Spacing, Span, Punct, TokenStream};
use quote::{TokenStreamExt, ToTokens};
pub struct Path {
    pub global: bool,
    pub segments: Vec<PathSegment>,
}
impl ToTokens for Path {
    fn to_tokens(&self, tokens: &mut TokenStream) {
        for (i, segment) in self.segments.iter().enumerate() {
            if i > 0 || self.global {
                // Double colon `::`
                tokens.append(Punct::new(':', Spacing::Joint));
                tokens.append(Punct::new(':', Spacing::Alone));
            }
            segment.to_tokens(tokens);
        }
    }
}
```

# quote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quote/latest/quote/

## Expand description

This crate provides the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for turning Rust syntax tree data
structures into tokens of source code.

Procedural macros in Rust receive a stream of tokens as input, execute arbitrary Rust code to determine how to manipulate those tokens, and produce a stream of tokens to hand back to the compiler to compile into the caller’s crate. Quasi-quoting is a solution to one piece of that — producing tokens to return to the compiler.

The idea of quasi-quoting is that we write *code* that we treat as *data*.
Within the `quote!` macro, we can write what looks like code to our text
editor or IDE. We get all the benefits of the editor’s brace matching,
syntax highlighting, indentation, and maybe autocompletion. But rather than
compiling that as code into the current crate, we can treat it as data, pass
it around, mutate it, and eventually hand it back to the compiler as tokens
to compile into the macro caller’s crate.

This crate is motivated by the procedural macro use case, but is a general-purpose Rust quasi-quoting library and is not specific to procedural macros.

```
[dependencies]
quote = "1.0"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following quasi-quoted block of code is something you might find in [a](https://serde.rs/)
procedural macro having to do with data structure serialization. The `#var`
syntax performs interpolation of runtime variables into the quoted tokens.
Check out the documentation of the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for more detail about
the syntax. See also the

[macro which is important for implementing hygienic procedural macros.](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)

`quote_spanned!````
let tokens = quote! {
    struct SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        value: &'a #field_ty,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData<#item_ty>,
    }
    impl #generics serde::Serialize for SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
        where
            S: serde::Serializer,
        {
            #path(self.value, serializer)
        }
    }
    SerializeWith {
        value: #value,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData::<#item_ty>,
    }
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-macro-code-generators)Non-macro code generators

When using `quote` in a build.rs or main.rs and writing the output out to a
file, consider having the code generator pass the tokens through
[prettyplease](https://github.com/dtolnay/prettyplease) before writing. This way if an error occurs in the generated
code it is convenient for a human to read and debug.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [format_](https://docs.rs/macro.format_ident.html)- ident
- Formatting macro for constructing `Ident`s.
- [quote](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html)
- The whole point.
- [quote_](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)- spanned
- Same as `quote!`, but applies a given span to all tokens originating within the macro invocation.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Ident](https://docs.rs/trait.IdentFragment.html)- Fragment
- Specialized formatting trait used by `format_ident!`.
- [ToTokens](https://docs.rs/trait.ToTokens.html)
- Types that can be interpolated inside a `quote!`invocation.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/trait.TokenStreamExt.html)- Stream - Ext
- TokenStream extension trait with methods for appending tokens.

# proc-macro2 1.0.106 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/proc-macro2/^1.0.80

# proc-macro2

A wrapper around the procedural macro API of the compiler's `proc_macro` crate.
This library serves two purposes:

-
**Bring proc-macro-like functionality to other contexts like build.rs and main.rs.**Types from`proc_macro`are entirely specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a procedural macro. Meanwhile`proc_macro2`types may exist anywhere including non-macro code. By developing foundational libraries like[syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn)and[quote](https://github.com/dtolnay/quote)against`proc_macro2`rather than`proc_macro`, the procedural macro ecosystem becomes easily applicable to many other use cases and we avoid reimplementing non-macro equivalents of those libraries.
-
**Make procedural macros unit testable.**As a consequence of being specific to procedural macros, nothing that uses`proc_macro`can be executed from a unit test. In order for helper libraries or components of a macro to be testable in isolation, they must be implemented using`proc_macro2`.

## Usage

```
[]
 = "1.0"
```
The skeleton of a typical procedural macro typically looks like this:

```
extern crate proc_macro;
```
If parsing with [Syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn), you'll use [ parse_macro_input!](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/macro.parse_macro_input.html) instead to propagate
parse errors correctly back to the compiler when parsing fails.

## Unstable features

The default feature set of proc-macro2 tracks the most recent stable compiler
API. Functionality in `proc_macro` that is not yet stable is not exposed by
proc-macro2 by default.

To opt into the additional APIs available in the most recent nightly compiler,
the `procmacro2_semver_exempt` config flag must be passed to rustc. We will
polyfill those nightly-only APIs back to Rust 1.68.0. As these are unstable APIs
that track the nightly compiler, minor versions of proc-macro2 may make breaking
changes to them at any time.

```
RUSTFLAGS='--cfg procmacro2_semver_exempt' cargo build
```
Note that this must not only be done for your crate, but for any crate that depends on your crate. This infectious nature is intentional, as it serves as a reminder that you are outside of the normal semver guarantees.

Semver exempt methods are marked as such in the proc-macro2 documentation.

---

# rustversion 1.0.22 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rustversion/^1.0

# Compiler version cfg

This crate provides macros for conditional compilation according to rustc
compiler version, analogous to [ #[cfg(...)]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg-attribute) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg_attr-attribute)

`#[cfg_attr(...)]````
[]
 = "1.0"
```
## Selectors

-
`#[rustversion::stable]`— True on any stable compiler.
-
`#[rustversion::stable(1.34)]`— True on exactly the specified stable compiler.
-
`#[rustversion::beta]`— True on any beta compiler.
-
`#[rustversion::nightly]`— True on any nightly compiler or dev build.
-
`#[rustversion::nightly(2025-01-01)]`— True on exactly one nightly.
-
`#[rustversion::since(1.34)]`— True on that stable release and any later compiler, including beta and nightly.
-
`#[rustversion::since(2025-01-01)]`— True on that nightly and all newer ones.
-
`#[rustversion::before(`version or date`)]`— Negative of*#[rustversion::since(...)]*.
-
`#[rustversion::not(`selector`)]`— Negative of any selector; for example*#[rustversion::not(nightly)]*.
-
`#[rustversion::any(`selectors...`)]`— True if any of the comma-separated selectors is true; for example*#[rustversion::any(stable, beta)]*.
-
`#[rustversion::all(`selectors...`)]`— True if all of the comma-separated selectors are true; for example*#[rustversion::all(since(1.31), before(1.34))]*.
-
`#[rustversion::attr(`selector`,`attribute`)]`— For conditional inclusion of attributes; analogous to`cfg_attr`.
-
`rustversion::cfg!(`selector`)`— An expression form of any of the above attributes; for example*if rustversion::cfg!(any(stable, beta)) { ... }*.

## Use cases

Providing additional trait impls as types are stabilized in the standard library
without breaking compatibility with older compilers; in this case Pin<P>
stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2019/02/28/Rust-1.33.0.html#pinning):

```
use Pin;
```
Similar but for language features; the ability to control alignment greater than
1 of packed structs was stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/RELEASES.md#version-1330-2019-02-28).

```
;
```
Augmenting code with `const` as const impls are stabilized in the standard
library. This use of `const` as an attribute is recognized as a special case by
the rustversion::attr macro.

```
use Duration;
```
Emitting Cargo cfg directives from a build script. Note that this requires
listing `rustversion` under `[build-dependencies]` in Cargo.toml, not
`[dependencies]`.

```
// build.rs
```
```
// src/lib.rs
extern crate alloc;
```
